content: In human anatomy, the term hamstring refers to one of the tendons that define the boundaries of the space located behind the knee. In modern anatomical terminology, the term typically refers to the tendons of three specific muscles: the semitendinosus, the semimembranosus, and the biceps femoris. In quadrupedal animals, the hamstring refers to a single, large tendon located behind the knee or a comparable anatomical region. In humans, the hamstring is situated along the posterior aspect of the femur, as illustrated in anatomical diagrams. The term ham historically referred to the fatty tissue and muscle located behind the knee, while string refers to the tendons. Together, the term hamstrings describes the string-like tendons that can be palpated on either side of the back of the knee. The posterior thigh contains four muscles that contribute to knee flexion (bending). Of these, three also extend (straighten) the hip joint. However, the short head of the biceps femoris, due to its distinct origin and innervation, does not participate in hip extension and is therefore sometimes excluded from the definition of the hamstring group. The hamstrings span and act upon two major joints: the hip and the knee. The semitendinosus and semimembranosus muscles extend the hip when the trunk is stabilized or extend the trunk when the hip is fixed. These muscles also flex the knee and medially (inwardly) rotate the lower leg when the knee is bent. The long head of the biceps femoris assists in hip extension, such as during the initiation of walking. Both the short and long heads of the biceps femoris flex the knee and laterally (outwardly) rotate the lower leg when the knee is bent. The hamstrings are essential for various daily activities, including walking, running, jumping, and controlling certain trunk movements. During walking, the hamstrings primarily function as antagonists to the quadriceps, helping to decelerate knee extension. A hamstring strain, commonly referred to as a pulled hamstring, occurs when the muscle fibers and associated tissues are excessively stretched or torn. Grade I Hamstring Strain: In a grade one strain, symptoms may not become apparent until after the activity has concluded. The individual may experience a sensation of cramping or tightness, along with mild pain when the muscle is stretched or contracted. This type of injury is sometimes colloquially referred to as a pulled hammy. Grade II Hamstring Strain: A grade two strain is characterized by immediate and more intense pain compared to a grade one injury. Pain is elicited upon stretching or contracting the muscle, and the affected area is typically tender to the touch. Grade III Hamstring Strain: A grade three strain represents a severe injury in which the muscle is completely torn. This results in immediate, sharp, or burning pain, and the individual is unable to walk without significant discomfort. A noticeable lump of muscle tissue may form above a depression at the site of the tear. Within a few days, bruising may develop below the injury site due to internal bleeding. The initial management of any muscle injury, including hamstring strains, involves the RICE protocol: rest, ice, compression, and elevation. Ice should never be applied directly to the skin. This approach aims to minimize bleeding and tissue damage. Rest is particularly critical, as ignoring this step can exacerbate the injury, potentially worsening a grade one strain to a grade two or a grade two strain to a grade three. For grade one strains, a recovery period of approximately three weeks is recommended before resuming athletic activities. Grade two strains typically require four to six weeks of rest. In cases of complete muscle rupture (grade three), surgical repair is necessary, followed by a rehabilitation period of approximately three months. Regardless of the severity of the injury, the initial five days of treatment are consistent. The affected leg should be rested in an elevated position, with an ice pack applied for 20 minutes every two hours, if feasible. A compression bandage should be used to reduce bleeding and swelling. After the initial five-day period of rest, more active rehabilitation can begin. The distal tendon of the semitendinosus muscle is frequently utilized in surgical procedures, such as anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. During this procedure, a segment of the tendon is harvested to replace the damaged ACL, which is one of the four primary ligaments stabilizing the knee joint.
